# Case study: the BR-116 catchment {#sec-m2-estudo-de-caso}

The question of this chapter is a recurring request in any transport planning
department:

> *How many people live in the catchment of a federal highway segment, how are they
> distributed across municipalities, and how many of them are less than 5 km from the axis?*

It is the task normally solved in QGIS with *buffer* + intersection + sum of attributes.
We will do the same in code, with official data, and with the pitfalls explained.

The segment chosen is the **BR-116 where it crosses the Serra do Mar**, between the Curitiba Metropolitan
Region and the coast: steep terrain, concentrated settlement and a logistics corridor that
links the Port of Paranaguá to the interior. But the steps in this chapter work for any
highway well mapped in OSM: only the value of `ref` in the query and the bounding box
(`bbox`) of the segment change. Some options to redo the exercise with another highway:

```{r}
rodovias_sugeridas <- data.frame(
  br     = c("BR-116", "BR-101", "BR-153", "BR-262", "BR-381"),
  segment = c("Serra do Mar, Curitiba-coast",
             "Santa Catarina coast, Florianópolis-Joinville",
             "Transbrasiliana, segment in Goiás",
             "Serra do Espinhaço, Vitória-Belo Horizonte",
             "Fernão Dias, São Paulo-Belo Horizonte"),
  uf     = c("PR/SC", "SC", "GO", "ES/MG", "SP/MG"),
  reason = c("steep terrain, corridor to the Port of Paranaguá (this chapter's example)",
             "coastal axis, almost continuous urban settlement",
             "long, low-density highway, a contrast with an urban segment",
             "iron ore corridor, mountainous terrain",
             "one of the busiest road corridors in the country")
)

knitr::kable(rodovias_sugeridas)
```

Pick a highway from the table (or look up the BR- code of the highway in your region) and redo the
chapter replacing `value = "BR-116"` with the chosen code and adjusting the `bbox` to the area of
interest. Here we carry on with the BR-116.

```{r}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# default basemap for mapview(): OpenStreetMap
mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery"))

crs_trabalho <- 31982    # SIRGAS 2000 / UTM 22S, in metres, to measure and buffer
```

## Step 1: The road axis

```{r}
arquivo_br116 <- "dados/brutos/br116_serra.gpkg"

if (!file.exists(arquivo_br116)) {
  consulta <- osmdata::opq(bbox = c(-49.40, -25.75, -48.40, -25.15), timeout = 120) |>
    osmdata::add_osm_feature(key = "ref", value = "BR-116") |>
    osmdata::osmdata_sf()

  sf::st_write(
    consulta$osm_lines |>
      dplyr::select(dplyr::any_of(c("osm_id", "name", "ref", "highway", "lanes", "maxspeed"))) |>
      sf::st_transform(4674),
    arquivo_br116, quiet = TRUE
  )
}

br116 <- sf::st_read(arquivo_br116, quiet = TRUE) |> sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)

c(trechos = nrow(br116),
  extensao_km = round(as.numeric(sum(sf::st_length(br116))) / 1000, 1))
```

Note that the summed length is greater than the real length of the corridor: OSM has separate
carriageways, slip roads and frontage roads as distinct features. To measure corridor length
this would need handling; to define a **catchment**, it does no harm,
because `st_union()` dissolves the overlap.

```{r}
eixo <- sf::st_union(br116)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The official version of this step

In a product for publication, the axis does not come from OSM, but from **DNIT's SNV**, which has
the BR code, segment, jurisdiction and carriageway status.

```{r}
#| eval: false
snv <- sf::st_read("dados/brutos/snv/SNV_202601A.shp", quiet = TRUE) |>
  sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)

eixo <- snv |>
  dplyr::filter(vl_br == "116", sg_uf %in% c("PR", "SC")) |>
  sf::st_union()
```

The rest of the chapter is identical. What changes is the citation of the source in the report. The names of the
SNV columns change between versions; run `names(snv)` first.
:::

## Step 2: The catchment bands

```{r}
faixas <- c(2000, 5000, 10000)

influencia <- lapply(faixas, \(d) {
  sf::st_buffer(eixo, dist = d) |>
    sf::st_as_sf() |>
    dplyr::mutate(faixa_m = d)
})

influencia <- influencia |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::rename(geom = x) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(faixa_m))     # largest to smallest, to draw in layers

# area of each band, in a separate table
area_km2 <- units::set_units(sf::st_area(influencia), km^2)

tabela_faixas <- sf::st_drop_geometry(influencia)
tabela_faixas$area_km2 <- round(as.numeric(area_km2), 1)

knitr::kable(tabela_faixas)
```

Three bands, not one, because the question "who is affected" rarely has a single answer:
2 km is the immediate neighbourhood, 5 km is the area of direct access, 10 km is the economic
area of influence. Presenting all three leaves the decision to whoever reads the report.

Before moving on, check visually that the bands cover the expected corridor:

```{r}
mapview::mapview(influencia, zcol = "faixa_m") + mapview::mapview(br116)
```

## Step 3: Population from the IBGE statistical grid

To sum population inside an irregular polygon, the ideal data are those with the **smallest unit
possible**. We will use the IBGE statistical grid, in which each cell has the resident
population. That way, the sum inside the band is direct, without having to split census tracts.

```{r}
arquivo_grade <- "dados/brutos/grade_pr.gpkg"

if (!file.exists(arquivo_grade)) {
  grade_pr <- geobr::read_statistical_grid(year = 2022, code_muni = "PR", showProgress = FALSE)
  sf::st_write(grade_pr, arquivo_grade, quiet = TRUE)
}

grade <- sf::st_read(arquivo_grade, quiet = TRUE) |> sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)

dim(grade)
names(grade)
```

```{r}
# spatial crop by the largest band, done before any calculation:
# it cuts hundreds of thousands of cells down to what matters
maior_faixa <- influencia |> dplyr::filter(faixa_m == max(faixa_m))

grade_recorte <- grade[sf::st_intersects(grade, maior_faixa, sparse = FALSE)[, 1], ]
nrow(grade_recorte)
```

```{r}
# the grid's population column
pop_col <- dplyr::intersect(c("pop_total", "POP", "pop"), names(grade_recorte))[1]
grade_recorte <- grade_recorte |> dplyr::mutate(pop = as.numeric(.data[[pop_col]]))

c(celulas = nrow(grade_recorte), populacao_total = sum(grade_recorte$pop, na.rm = TRUE))
```

There are thousands of cells, too heavy for `mapview` to draw at once. To see what the
grid actually looks like, a sample is enough: the cells within 3 km of a point on the axis, on the way out
of Curitiba.

```{r}
ponto_eixo <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_point(c(-49.2066, -25.3895)), crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)

parcela_grade <- grade_recorte[
  sf::st_is_within_distance(grade_recorte, ponto_eixo, dist = 3000, sparse = FALSE)[, 1], ]

mapview::mapview(parcela_grade, zcol = "pop", layer.name = "Population per cell") +
  mapview::mapview(br116, color = "#b3402a", lwd = 3, layer.name = "BR-116")
```

Click on a cell to see its attributes: each square has an identifier and the resident
population. The smaller cells are in urban areas, where the IBGE grid is finer.

::: {.callout-important}
## Why not use the census tract directly

Census tracts are larger than the grid cells, and the catchment cuts most
of them in half. Summing the population of the tracts **touched** overestimates; summing only the
tracts **entirely inside** underestimates. The correct way out, when tracts are used, is
**area weighting**: assuming the population is spread evenly within the tract.

```{r}
#| eval: false
setores <- geobr::read_census_tract(code_tract = "PR", year = 2010,
                                    simplified = FALSE, showProgress = FALSE) |>
  sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho) |>
  dplyr::left_join(pop_por_setor, by = "code_tract")     # population from censobr

ponderado <- setores |>
  dplyr::mutate(area_total = sf::st_area(geom)) |>
  sf::st_intersection(maior_faixa) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    fracao = as.numeric(sf::st_area(geom) / area_total),
    pop_na_faixa = pop * fracao
  )

sum(ponderado$pop_na_faixa)
```

This assumption is fragile in large rural tracts. That is precisely why the statistical
grid, with much smaller cells, gives a better result for rights-of-way and catchment
areas. Record in the report which method was used.
:::

## Step 4: Population by band

```{r}
pop_por_faixa <- lapply(sort(faixas), \(d) {
  f <- influencia |> dplyr::filter(faixa_m == d)
  dentro <- grade_recorte[sf::st_intersects(grade_recorte, f, sparse = FALSE)[, 1], ]
  data.frame(
    faixa_m   = d,
    celulas   = nrow(dentro),
    populacao = sum(dentro$pop, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    area_km2 = as.numeric(units::set_units(
      sf::st_area(influencia$geom[match(faixa_m, influencia$faixa_m)]), km^2)),
    densidade = populacao / area_km2
  )

pop_por_faixa |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    `Band (km)` = faixa_m / 1000,
    `Area (km²)` = round(area_km2, 1),
    `Population`  = scales::comma(populacao),
    `Inhab./km²`   = round(densidade, 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "rrrr")
```

Density falling as the band widens is the expected and informative result: settlement
is concentrated next to the axis.

## Step 5: Distribution by municipality

```{r}
arquivo <- "dados/brutos/muni_pr_sc.gpkg"
if (!file.exists(arquivo)) {
  muni <- dplyr::bind_rows(
    geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "PR", year = 2022, showProgress = FALSE),
    geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = "SC", year = 2022, showProgress = FALSE)
  )
  sf::st_write(muni, arquivo, quiet = TRUE)
}
muni <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE) |> sf::st_transform(crs_trabalho)

faixa5 <- influencia |> dplyr::filter(faixa_m == 5000)

pop_muni <- grade_recorte[sf::st_intersects(grade_recorte, faixa5, sparse = FALSE)[, 1], ] |>
  # the grid already has IBGE's code_muni/name_muni; we drop them to avoid
  # a name clash with the join below, which is the source we want to use
  dplyr::select(pop) |>
  # the join uses the CENTRE of each cell: with st_intersects, cells on the border
  # would be counted in two municipalities and the total population would double
  sf::st_point_on_surface() |>
  sf::st_join(muni |> dplyr::select(code_muni, name_muni, abbrev_state)) |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  dplyr::summarise(populacao = sum(pop, na.rm = TRUE),
            celulas = dplyr::n(),
            .by = c(code_muni, name_muni, abbrev_state)) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(code_muni)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(populacao))

pop_muni |>
  dplyr::mutate(part = populacao / sum(populacao)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Municipality = name_muni, State = abbrev_state,
            `Population in the 5 km band` = scales::comma(populacao),
            `Share (%)` = scales::percent(part, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "llrr")
```

Note the join by the cell's centre and the preserved IBGE code: it is what lets you take this result
to any other municipal dataset (GDP, vehicle fleet, tax revenue) with module 1's `left_join`.

## Step 6: The map

```{r}
#| label: fig-caso-faixa
#| fig-cap: "BR-116 catchment bands in the Serra do Mar and resident population per cell"
#| fig-height: 5.6
recorte_vis <- sf::st_bbox(influencia |> dplyr::filter(faixa_m == 10000))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = muni, fill = "grey98", colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = grade_recorte |> dplyr::filter(pop > 0),
          aes(fill = pop), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = influencia, fill = NA, colour = "#1a5b8a",
          linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_sf(data = br116, colour = "#b3402a", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1, transform = "log10",
                       name = "Population\nper cell") +
  coord_sf(xlim = recorte_vis[c("xmin", "xmax")],
           ylim = recorte_vis[c("ymin", "ymax")], expand = FALSE) +
  ggspatial::annotation_scale(location = "bl", width_hint = 0.25) +
  labs(
    title = "BR-116 / Serra do Mar: 2, 5 and 10 km catchment bands",
    caption = paste("Sources: road axis OpenStreetMap; population IBGE, statistical grid.",
                    "Own elaboration.")
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 10) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))
```

The map above covers the whole corridor, which leaves little room to see detail where
settlement is densest. A second map, zoomed in on the Curitiba area, shows the
distribution of population in the cells near the start of the corridor better:

```{r}
#| label: fig-caso-faixa-curitiba
#| fig-cap: "Zoom on the Curitiba area: same catchment and population per cell"
#| fig-height: 5.2
zoom_curitiba <- muni |>
  dplyr::filter(name_muni == "Curitiba") |>
  sf::st_buffer(8000) |>
  sf::st_bbox()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = muni, fill = "grey98", colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = grade_recorte |> dplyr::filter(pop > 0),
          aes(fill = pop), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = influencia, fill = NA, colour = "#1a5b8a",
          linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  # white outline underneath + thick line on top: the highway stands out from the grid
  geom_sf(data = br116, colour = "white", linewidth = 3) +
  geom_sf(data = br116, colour = "#1a5b8a", linewidth = 1.6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1, transform = "log10",
                       name = "Population\nper cell") +
  coord_sf(xlim = zoom_curitiba[c("xmin", "xmax")],
           ylim = zoom_curitiba[c("ymin", "ymax")], expand = FALSE) +
  ggspatial::annotation_scale(location = "bl", width_hint = 0.25) +
  labs(title = "Detail: start of the corridor, Curitiba area") +
  theme_void(base_size = 10) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))
```

## Step 7: Export

```{r}
#| eval: false
dir.create("resultados", showWarnings = FALSE)

# spatial layers, in a single GeoPackage, in the official CRS
sf::st_write(sf::st_transform(influencia, 4674),  "resultados/br116_faixas.gpkg",
         layer = "faixas_influencia", delete_dsn = TRUE)
sf::st_write(sf::st_transform(br116, 4674),       "resultados/br116_faixas.gpkg",
         layer = "eixo_br116", append = TRUE)

# tables for the report
writexl::write_xlsx(
  list("Por faixa" = pop_por_faixa, "Por município" = pop_muni),
  "resultados/br116_populacao.xlsx"
)
```

## What this case study showed

1. The *buffer* → clip → sum workflow, which in GIS is a sequence of clicks, is 15
   lines here. And those 15 lines can be run again for another BR by changing one filter.
2. The choice of CRS is not a detail: a *buffer* in metres requires a metric projection, and checking
   the area (π r²) is the sanity test.
3. The unit of the population data determines the method: the statistical grid allows a direct sum;
   census tracts require area weighting, and that must be written in the report.
4. The IBGE code, preserved by the spatial join, is the bridge to any other municipal
   dataset. That is exactly what we will do in module 3.
